speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS-REPORTED INCREASE IN CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister whether the report which appeared in the paper yesterday to the effect that a Canadian armoured unit is to be sent to the United Nations emergency force is correct? If so, may we have a statement concerning the proposal?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS-REPORTED INCREASE IN CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: If I may, Mr. Speaker, I will answer that question. subtopic: UNITED NATIONS-REPORTED INCREASE IN CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO EMERGENCY FORCE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Would the minister be willing to tell the house of any progress he may have made in evolving a plan to apply unemployment insurance to fishermen?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Gloucester told me that he intended to ask a question on this subject, and I think I should also say that the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart), the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) also spoke to me.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext: Put them all in.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext: I hope I have.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext:
And the hon. member for
Restigouche-Madawaska.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext: Where is he?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PLAN TO COVER FISHERMEN
speechtext:
In accordance with the forecast I made when the act was amended last session, an unemployment insurance plan for fishermen has been worked out and approved by the government.
The commission is now taking the necessary steps through its regional and appropriate local offices to have the plan commence on April 1 next for the collection of contributions into the fund, and to commence on January 1 next for a consideration of applications for benefit.
Under this plan commercial fishermen will be covered regardless of whether they are wage earners, or work on shares as coadventurers, or carry on their fishing operations alone. For those who are paid wages, the employer and the employee will, of course, make the contributions in the regular way.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Fishermen who do not work for wages have no employer in the ordinary sense. It will be necessary in their case for the person who first buys or acquires a fisherman's catch to be treated as the employer for the purpose of making the contributions and keeping the records.
In general, the rates of contributions and benefits will be the same as those applying to all other insured workers.
The period when benefit may be paid will be restricted to the time of year when most fishermen are unemployed. The plan, therefore, provides for the payment of benefit only between the beginning of January and the middle of April, for such number of weeks as the claimant may be entitled to, with a minimum of 10. Provision is made for integrating fishing contributions with contributions from other insured employment.
Contributions into the fund will commence as from April 1 next, but I wish to make it clear that these contributions will not count for any benefit until the beginning of January 1, 1958.
What I have given, Mr. Speaker, is just a general outline of the plan. I would be glad to give further details when my estimates are before the house.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON WORKING DAYS LOST THROUGH ILLNESS AND INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON WORKING DAYS LOST THROUGH ILLNESS AND INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer a question asked on January 24 last, as recorded at page 594 of Hansard. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) asked for the total number of man working days lost through illness as a supplement to the information that 1,261,400 man working days were lost through industrial disputes in 1956.
I said at the time that only an estimate could be given, and this is it. The best means of providing such an estimate appears to be through the monthly labour force survey. From this survey, information is obtained as to the number of persons with jobs who did not work during the survey week because of illness, and also the number of persons with jobs who worked less than 35 hours during the week because of illness. In the year 1956 the average number of persons who did not work at all during the survey week because of illness was 57,250 per week; the average who worked less than 35 hours because of illness was 26,750. Assuming that persons in the first category lost five days per week and persons in the second category lost two days per week, it has been estimated that in the year 1956 just under 17 million man days were lost owing to illness. The corresponding figure for 1955 would be just over 16 million.
In addition to this labour force survey the dominion bureau of statistics have crosschecked through other surveys which seem to indicate that the figures I have given may be slightly low.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Minister of Justice. In view of the fact that the merger between the British Columbia Sugar Refining Company Limited and the Manitoba Sugar Company Limited, which the report of the restrictive trade practices commission recommended should not take place, has already come into effect, what action does the government propose to take to break up this combine in the sugar industry in western Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: I am sure that my hon. friend is aware that all these combines cases involve as a rule very intricate facts and the conclusions arising out of these facts are complex. This report which has been received quite recently is being studied by the department and in due course I will be making a statement concerning it. Until this study is completed I have nothing to say in the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. When he is making that study will the minister ascertain whether or not the price increases made recently by the Manitoba Sugar Company were made on the initiative of that company itself or were they made at the dictation of the combine in western Canada which is headed by this British Columbia company?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: It is the practice in all of these cases to go over all the relevant material which is available and if this particular supposition which my hon. friend voices is the fact we will certainly endeavour to confirm it.

subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Am I correct in saying that this transaction just referred to is much similar to a transaction in the brewing industry about which similar warnings or cautions were sounded by the department? If so, what is the situation in that respect? Is the government taking any action, because I understand that that merger is now complete.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Any similarity between these two I should think would be rather superficial. In the case of the sugar merger the completed merger is alleged by the report to give the resulting corporation control of a large area of the trade. It was found in the beer report, as I am sure my hon. friend who asked the question is aware, that that result did not obtain after the transactions reported in the report had been completed. In that respect the two are quite different.

maintopic: BEER-ACTION TO BE TAKEN ON ALLEGED COMBINE IN WESTERN CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: BEER-ACTION TO BE TAKEN ON ALLEGED COMBINE IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. In view of the recommendation of the restrictive trade practices commission that the government should take steps to prevent Canadian Breweries Limited from acquiring control over Western Canada Brewers Limited, and in view of the action of Canadian Breweries Limited in extending its control over Western Canada Brewers, what action is the minister taking to carry out the recommendation of the restrictive trade practices commission in order to prevent the formation of a brewery monopoly in western Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BEER-ACTION TO BE TAKEN ON ALLEGED COMBINE IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I wish to thank my hon. friend for having given me notice of his question. The report of the restrictive trade practices commission expressed the opinion that the merger program of Canadian Breweries Limited had been monopolistic in nature and not in the public interest. It also came to the conclusion, however, that Canadian Breweries Limited had not acquired complete or substantial control over the industry in any part of Canada.
Since then, that is since the delivery of the report, the court of appeal in British Columbia has handed down a decision in a Vancouver gasoline case which, if correct, would appear to cast some doubt on whether there is a good case for prosecution in the beer case. The Department of Justice immediately applied to the Supreme Court of Canada for leave to appeal against the British Columbia decision, but the application was refused in October last. A similar point, however, is before the Supreme Court of Canada in the fine paper case. The point is, however, generally speaking, whether substantial elimination of competition constitutes injury to the public under the anti-combines legislation. This is one of the points upon which our decision as to what to do in the beer case turns, and we would prefer not to come to a conclusion in the beer case upon the other point until the fine papers case shall have been decided.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are three or four questions I should like to ask the Prime Minister concerning this resolution, and the first is this. In 1953 when we had some discussion about the functions of the Canada Council the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 4431 of Hansard for April 27 of that year:
There are other matters, too. At one time consideration was given to a Canadian order or medal.

Canada Council
I think the Canada Council, if there should come to be one, should have the initiative of recommendations in that regard . . .
It would be interesting if the Prime Minister would tell the committee today whether it is the intention of the government to make provision for the Canada medal and whether one of the functions of this council would be to make the awards. Also would he tell us what type of scholarships the government has in mind? The Massey commission as I read their report recommended that there should be post-graduate scholarships, fellowships, exchange scholarships presumably for graduates from other countries and, finally, undergraduate scholarships. In at least two of those recommendations mention was made of scholarships in the humanities, the social sciences and law. Is it the intention that there shall be these four different types of scholarships or even more and are they to be restricted to the humanities, the social sciences and the law?
The third question is this. What if any provision is made for advancing the training of engineers and scientists under the work of this council? And finally, would the Prime Minister explain why there is to be a fund set up of $50 million rather than an annual grant? He did deal with that briefly when he spoke on January 18 and I am referring to page 396 of Hansard for that date, but I think it would be helpful if we were told in more detail just why the system of setting aside a large sum of money is being followed. I ask that particularly because, as the Prime Minister knows the Massey commission did not make a recommendation of that kind but on the contrary recommended an annual grant. At page 382 of the report of the Massey commission we find these words:
We do not find it possible to propose specific sums; we should, however, imagine that the council would find it possible to perform its varied duties effectively with an annual budget which would constitute a very slight charge upon all members of the Canadian population. We venture to believe that our fellow-citizens would find this investment modest in relation to the returns which, we are confident, they could reasonably expect.
If that recommendation had been followed the result would be to keep parliament and through parliament the Canadian people much more directly in touch with the work of the council. This system of making an annual grant has been adopted in other cases. I think that is what is done in the case of the national research council. I believe they make provision for their scholarships out of their annual vote so there can be a discussion in parliament each session as that money is voted on the question of the scholarships that are being awarded by the national research council.

There seems to be a good deal of questioning as to the wisdom of simply setting aside the sum of $50 million. Once that is done then it passes right beyond the reach of parliament. I submit that Mr. Massey and his fellow commissioners had in mind throughout the report having an annual payment. Perhaps the Prime Minister would be good enough to explain why the other system is being adopted.

The second question was, will there be any determination in the bill of the kind of scholarships that will be provided. There are no provisions or limitations in the bill in that regard except that there will have to be scholarships for the furthering of the objectives of the Canada Council which are to promote the development of the humanities and social sciences and there will be no scholarships for the development or promotion of engineering and scientific research. That is already being done and if it requires to be increased it should continue to be done through the national research council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Of course, the national research council does not train engineers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
No, the
national research council does not train engineers and we should not set up the Canada Council as a university to train engineers or to train any others. It is to give assistance to the institutions that do that work or through scholarships to those who would be benefiting from that work. It is not intended that the Canada Council should establish a school to train any person for advanced studies.

The fourth question was, why is there a fund of $50 million being appropriated at this time whilst that had not been a recommendation made by the Massey commission. That is probably something that went beyond what the Massey commission recommended at that time. It was for the purpose of creating this body in such a way that it would not be subject to frequent pressures in the allocation of the funds which would be placed at its disposal.
I might say that one of the considerations which I had in mind-it was not the governing consideration-was the fact that there had been at the time we were preparing this recommendation for parliament two very unusually large estates from which the collections of succession duties had been made in amounts that could not be considered to be recurring amounts. In connection with one estate the statement had been made more than once by the deceased during his lifetime that he was not making provision during his lifetime or apt to make any under his will for benefactions to public institutions because the succession duties were so high, the proportion of his estate which would be taken in succession duties, if it were thought fit, could be employed on the recommendation of the government by parliament for like purposes.
In the case of the other estate it is not to my knowledge that the deceased had made a similar declaration, but it is to my knowledge that he had made modest contributions to institutions of the character of those envisaged by this legislation. But they were amounts that were quite abnormal and that came into the revenues or incomes of the year when these matters were being considered. That was one of the factors which influenced my judgment in making the recommendation to my colleagues that the Canada Council be provided with this endowment which I hope rather confidently will be substantially increased by endowments from well-to-do Canadians, either as gifts or as a result of testamentary dispositions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Would they not be tax exempt?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: They would be tax exempt, yes. That was the rationalizing of the first of the two deceased I have mentioned who left abnormally large estates.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: To what estates is the Prime Minister referring?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
It is well known that they are the Killam and the Sir James Dunn estates. They were abnormally large estates. Mr. Killam had stated that if there was a bequest for one of these benefactions it would not incur succession duties,
Canada Council
but that if there was not the whole estate would incur succession duties and the government might appropriate such portion as it saw fit to the furtherance of the objectives of these foundations or endowments or institutions which had received consideration from wealthy citizens who felt that they were thus making some return to the Canadian society for the benefits they had reaped from the functioning of Canadian institutions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not think that this is setting a dangerous precedent? Are we to be led to believe that if anyone puts a provision in his will that he expects the proceeds of succession duties to go to a certain place the government, having acted in this way, would be under an obligation to do it again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
The government would be under no obligation; the government was under no obligation to do it. It did provide a sort of windfall which came I think at a most opportune time. I suppose there will be other windfalls because in spite of the rates of taxation there are growing fortunes in the hands of Canadian individuals, as the hon. gentleman well knows, although that is not based on his or my experience.
There are also other occasions of that kind, but the reason was that I did not feel that the list of those who might be getting scholarships should be a matter for discussion in any kind of political arena and the choice of the kind of scholarships that would be first provided would I hope be wisely made by those who would be selected to become members of this council. Personally I would feel that it was post-graduate work which was most urgent at the present time. The greatest need at the present time in the humanities and social sciences is to prepare a larger number of qualified professors to teach these sciences in our universities. The other measure providing for annual aid of $16 million to the universities might be of some assistance in making university professorships more attractive to the people who would give the best kind of service in professorships in universities.
I would hope that originally a large part of the revenue which would be produced by this endowment would be devoted to the purposes of providing a considerably larger number of qualified professors for the universities because there is going to be a considerably larger number of young men and women looking for the kind of higher education which the universities can provide. Still it was felt that that might not always be the case, that there might be some consideration given to whether or not in certain cases

Canada Council
there should be undergraduate scholarships. It must be remembered that while an endowment of $50 million may look to be quite substantial the revenue from it will not provide a large number of undergraduate scholarships in proportion to the number of undergraduates who will be frequenting our universities.
While the smaller number of scholarships for post-graduate work or even for fellowship scholarships or exchange scholarships with other universities might not loom very large, it might be percentagewise considerable when compared with the total number of qualified professors there are in Canadian universities for the teaching of these sciences. I am disclosing some of the provisions which will be in the bill. I hope it will not be very long before the bill is available to hon. members and I see no point in not doing so when members are personally interested in receiving that information.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks at this time, though I am not going to become involved in the type of discussion which has been going on; I think that can be left until the bill is before the house and the committee, and we know precisely what we are discussing so far as details are concerned.
I want to welcome the announcement by the government that it is now prepared to proceed with the creation of the Canada Council. I believe that such a council is long overdue, and I feel that the results of its work will fully justify the effort involved in setting it up, because we have a number

of examples of similar bodies which have brought about considerable benefits at other levels of government.
In Great Britain, of course, a similar body was set up several years ago. It is not my intention to refer, except in passing, to the Arts Council of Great Britain, but I do want to suggest that we in Saskatchewan have been fortunate in enjoying the work of the Saskatchewan Arts Board since 1947, and I feel that the type of work carried on by that board could well set an example to a federal body. I do not wish to go into any details with regard to the many activities carried on by the Saskatchewan Arts Board, but I may say that the board has concerned itself with providing opportunities for Saskatchewan talent to be enjoyed by Saskatchewan people. With that end in mind, concert tours were arranged in order to enable Saskatchewan musicians who had distinguished themselves in other parts of Canada, and, indeed, beyond Canada, to return to their native province and allow their fellow citizens in that province to enjoy their music.
Tours were also arranged for drama groups. A number of years ago the University Players were sponsored by that organization, and these players took good drama into many areas of the province which in normal circumstances would never have had the chance of seeing "live" stage productions. The board has also done considerable work in the field of the visual arts, in crafts and in literature. As one example of the work they carried on, I may say that they conducted a "writers' workshop" a number of years ago under the direction of the famous Canadian author W. O. Mitchell. This was, of course, designed to provide some opportunity for young people who desired to make a career in this field to obtain some of the knowledge required in order to pursue that endeavour.
I think the Saskatchewan Ants Board has *more than proven itself as a valuable contribution to the welfare of the province, and I would like to point this out: the people who oppose the idea of the Canada Council are very much inclined to talk about "forcing culture down people's throats" or to make such statements as: "You cannot buy culture." No one is going to disagree with regard to that. It is not a question of trying to "buy culture"; it is a question of providing a climate which will encourage the development of the artist, and this is essentially what the Saskatchewan Arts Board has sought to do during the years of its existence.
I believe this is something which we have to recognize at the present time in this modern industrial age when we are thinking in terms of automation and in terms of making proper use of leisure time; and I believe
Canada Council
that as part of our education we should develop the capacity to use this leisure time to the best possible advantage. Certainly, any move which will encourage the development of the artist in Canada is going to enable Canadians to take advantage of such opportunities to enjoy a richer and a fuller life.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the government has indicated some awareness of the need but I am not satisfied that it is fully cognizant of all that is involved in this question. It is all very well to talk about encouraging the arts. It is all very well to talk about the type of program about which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke when he introduced this resolution. But it seems to me that we must be prepared to get down to practical cases. We must do something for these people whose services are indispensable in such a program.
I am just going to refer to one specific example of what I mean. I received something in the mail a few weeks ago. I am sure all hon. members received it. I refer to bulletins from the Civil Service Commission of Canada. These two bulletins happened to be in the same envelope. That is the only reason I am using these two for purposes of comparison. I note that one of these bulletins is headed "Civil Service of Canada Requires Librarians". What are the salaries offered? They are $3,180 to $3,780. They are the salaries offered to graduate librarians. Here is what they require of these people who enter the government service:
Duties (Librarian 1)
Under supervision, to perform professional librarian duties such as reference work, cataloguing and classifying material, compilation of bibliographies, supervision of preparation of material for binding, obtaining data for requisitioning of new material, preparation of reports and correspondence; to train and supervise non-professional library employees; and to perform other related duties as required.
That is quite a tall order, Mr. Chairman. I am sure that we want to get the best people into that field of work. Then the bulletin goes on to describe the qualifications: Qualifications
A Bachelor's degree in Library Science in a course of recognized standing;
Personal suitability; satisfactory physical condition.
The latter is common in most of these requirements. Then the bulletin goes on to say this:
Note: A certificate or diploma in library science is not considered as the equivalent of degree standing in Library Science.
He must take a degree course which is a post-graduate course after the Bachelor's degree in arts. Then the note continues:
For some positions a knowledge of French and/or one or more foreign languages may be required.

Canada Council
I think you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that the requirements for this job are quite high. Yet for this position the government is offering to pay the miserable pittance of $3,180 to $3,780. They want graduate librarians, persons who have gone through university and obtained their Bachelor's degree, who have gone through a school of library science and all they are offering such people is $3,180.
The other bulletin to which I referred a moment ago is here in my hand. I have no particular reason for picking this one out other than the fact that the two came together but I think it makes a startling contrast. This one is headed "Civil Service of Canada requires Real Estate Assessor". For one classification they offer $3,900 to $4,500 and for another classification, namely technical officer 3, they offer $4,710 to $5,310. What are the requirements for this particular job? They are stated here as follows:
A good general education acquired as a result of general training and experience; . . .
There is no talk of university degrees. There are no great requirements in so far as academic standing is concerned. Yet the salaries are vastly higher than are those offered to people whom we require to have a degree in library science.
If the government is going to indicate its sincerity in its desire to improve conditions in this field, the field with which we are concerned in this resolution, it seems to me that the government must take some cognizance of the need for bringing into line with present realities the salaries of the people who are needed to carry on this program. It seems to me that you cannot expect to undertake the program as envisaged in this resolution if you are not prepared to do the right thing by the type of people you want to attract into the government service. In this field of the Canada Council and the whole related field I cannot think of any more important personnel than the librarians because certainly the library is the focal point of any program which might be envisaged under this plan. In all sincerity I suggest to the government that if they are willing to face up to the need for doing something in this field, it is time they did something about these miserably low salaries.
I realize that we perhaps get applicants for these jobs. In spite of the fact that the salaries are so low, I think these people apply because they are intensely interested in this work. But in order to be fair I think we should not take advantage of them and ask these people to subsidize any program by taking wages which are materially lower than those which they could receive if they

entered into other fields of endeavour with the same amount of university training. I think it is a fair request to make that if we are really prepared to go ahead with such a program we must recognize the role which the library plays. Here is one instance in which I think the government could indicate its awareness of the problem before us.
There are other aspects of this matter with which I should like to deal in a general way but I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee this afternoon. However, I want to make one reference to the question of assistance to the universities. I realize that in the estimates the other day there was an item dealing with an increase in the per capita grant from 50 cents to one dollar. I realize that in this resolution there is some reference to the establishment of the university capital grant fund. But I think there must be some recognition of the need for an over-all program to assist our universities, not a piece-meal sort of arrangement where there is a little bit of assistance granted in this particular field and further assistance granted in some other field. I think there must be a general recognition of the role played by the university in our modern society. I do not think that the government have indicated that they are fully aware of the extent of the problem. I would also say this. You cannot isolate the university from the other fields of education. No matter how much assistance might be granted to the universities, if there is not some recognition of the need for assistance to the elementary and the secondary schools, then of course that program is not going to bring about the maximum results.
I think that the Canadian Labour Congress, in the brief presented to the cabinet the other day, referred to that question quite accurately when, under the heading of "Education", they stated as follows:
The situation in education in Canada at all levels from kindergarten to university has reached the proportions of a national emergency. The problems are acute. If the needs of a growing population requiring more and more education and training in an expanding economy are to be met adequately, the government of Canada will have to share the responsibility with the provinces for marshalling the necessary resources.
Then the congress sums the matter up by suggesting a practical method of going about meeting this problem. They do it in this
way:
We ask the government of Canada to convene a dominion-provincial conference on education to consider the problem and possible ways in which federal assistance can be provided.
We have been discussing the universities as though they are a problem apart. I think the number of youngsters who go through

our elementary schools, the quality of the education they receive and the number of graduates from our secondary schools, of course, will determine the effectiveness of any university program in the years which lie ahead. The problem is an immense one.
I think we must consider the proposal which is now before the house in terms of the problem which it professes to meet in part at least. As far as the universities are concerned, we now know that the annual operating costs are about $105 million in terms of increased population. We know that over the next ten years there is going to be required over $300 million in new construction and for operating costs an amount of $1,800 million. That, of course, is based on the assumption that the university population as a ratio to the general population has not increased. But-and this is very important-if we are going to keep pace in the modern world we must increase the number of young people who go on to university.
In order to do that it would require a still further expansion in the plant facilities throughout this country. The university population now stands at about 70,000, and it has been estimated that by 1966, on the present ratio of students to the rest of the population, the university population would amount to about 130,000. If we are going to keep pace with the rest of the world we have to increase that number to something in the neighbourhood of 300,000 students. This will require further construction costing around $850 million and, of course, further extensive operating costs.
When one considers the problem facing our universities, one comes to the conclusion we have to dismiss from our minds any suggestion that by granting the type of assistance outlined in this resolution or even including the increase in the per capita grant from 50 cents to $1 per capita, as outlined in the supplementary estimates the other day, we are going to meet the problem. The government has to face up to the whole problem and that problem has to be met by a comprehensive program aimed at granting assistance to education at all levels. If we do not do that, if we simply go about attacking the problem in a piecemeal fashion, we are going to find ourselves falling farther behind in the output of university graduates. In so far as the resolution does provide for the setting up of the Canada Council which will bring about many of the benefits we desire, and because there is at least an increased measure of assistance to education at the university level, the resolution certainly deserves the support of all members of the house.
Canada Council

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I have a few general remarks I wish to make on this resolution. It is some time since it was first introduced to the house, and I have been giving the subject considerable thought since that time. I must say that it is one of those things that the more a person thinks about it the less he thinks of it. I have read with a great deal of interest the introductory speeches, you might call them, by the leaders of the various groups. Of course, the Leader of the Opposition has taken the usual stand that the opposition is there to out liberal the Liberals. We have seen the socialists take a stand at which we are not surprised.
In dealing with this matter there are many avenues from which we could approach it. We hear quite a lot about culture. I must admit that it is something about which I know very little. If I were asked to give a definition of culture, I am sure that I would be at a loss. However, I profess to be an average Canadian with an average education. I like to read some good books and occasionally I do not mind reading one of those paperbacked novels. I enjoy a work of art. I must say that so far as modern art is concerned-I think they call it abstract or something of that nature-I do not understand it. I must admit, therefore, I am not very well steeped in culture.
However, there is one avenue from which we can approach the subject, but I am not going to devote much time to it. There were a couple of phrases which the Prime Minister used in his speech the other day and, to use a slang expression, they made me sit up and take notice. One of those phrases was "spiritual development". I would hesitate to think that we in this country are going to set up an organization that will usurp the functions of the various churches and spiritual organizations that we have. Another phrase that he used was "intellectual world brotherhood". Brotherhood, Mr. Chairman, suggests to me unity and harmony. Putting those phrases together, it would appear that we are going to try to develop harmony with the various other cultures in different parts of the world. We might say that some of these other cultures are not intellectual. Then, we say, who is to say, and what is the definition that will be given?
Are we in harmony, for instance, with the culture in Russia? If we are going to have a world brotherhood, can we eliminate part of the world or are we going to be in harmony with cultures throughout the world and in all their different phases? We can also think of the experiments in state culture. In the not too distant past we had one experiment which was spelled with a "K",

Canada Council
in a country that prided itself on culture. Yet, when the culture came under the control of the state we know that millions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of lives were sacrificed to try to eradicate the effect of that culture from the face of the globe. However, I am not going to labour that because I have a lot of faith in the people of Canada. I believe they will not be led too far afield in their ideologies or too far from their love and respect for personal freedom.
Then, reference was made to the humanities. I tried to ascertain what the Prime Minister meant the other day by his definition of the humanities, but I am afraid I am not much wiser. However, I should like to think of it more as humanitarian. The social sciences I should like to think of as engendering policies that would promote social welfare, family unity, family associations and all those things that go to build up a better way of life for the people of our country.
We heard something about a proper climate from the speaker who just took his seat. He made a worth-while contribution in telling us that we have to have the proper climate before a thing can flourish and grow. He mentioned the Saskatchewan Arts Board, I believe it was, the chief function of which was arranging tours for the works of the artists of that province. In other words, the Saskatchewan Arts Board was making it possible for the artists of Saskatchewan to earn a livelihood. The other day the hon. member for Mackenzie was quite concerned about the number of Canadian artists who were forced to leave this land of ours and go to the south or to Europe because they were unable to earn a living in this country. I would say; if those people are unable to earn a living in this country, then why promote more artists? Why spend money in educating more artists when you have not got a climate in this country at the present time to support those artists? I am sure that we could spend our money to much better advantage than putting through our education mills a number of people in excess of those who can earn a living in this country today.
I say that the holding of a diploma from an arts school or being a qualified dancer will not make your living any less costly or keep you from suffering the pangs of hunger. You must have the dollars and cents to buy the wherewithal on which to live and you must get it from the climate or from the field which is created in the country. In other words, the people of this country, the common Joes who go to the concerts and who listen to these people, have to contribute the livelihood that these people

require and to which they are entitled. I do not deny that fact. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would say that the first duty of this government is to create in Canada a field in which artists can grow, flourish and prosper. In order to do that I think it will require three steps. We must have assistance given to our whole educational program, starting right at the very bottom. I am surprised that many of the speakers in the debate thus far have coupled with this resolution assistance to universities on a general basis. Yet I know they must know by reading the resolution, that the assistance is certainly going to be very narrow. They speak of university extension, of university bursaries, fellowships, and so on, but they do not couple with that the fact that the bursaries and the assistance the government is going to give will create more artists which the climate of this country cannot support. They also fail to take into consideration the fact that the $50 million to be given to universities is to go for extensions not for dental colleges, or colleges that will turn out trained professional men who are badly needed in medicine and iri other professions. It will not turn out engineers. It will build additions and provide equipment that will promote the furtherance of the education of those taking courses in the fine arts. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say that the first of the three steps that we must consider is assistance to basic education. Our people must have a general education. I maintain that is the first requisite in order to give our citizens a little better appreciation of the finer things of life. This will require financial and advisory assistance and it will take all the resources this country can provide. It could start with the little red school house and follow up through all the levels of education, riot excluding the universities.
I do not want any person to misunderstand me. I am not opposed to university education. We are sadly lacking in it at the present time and we are lacking in facilities. When I speak of education in that sense I am more concerned with general education than with the narrow limits prescribed by this resolution.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar refer in his speech the other day to auditoriums that are so widely built in England. Anyway, I would agree with him that the finest addition to a public school building is an auditorium. I say to the committee it is rather strange that we have to go to the west to cite these examples, but the two western provinces are perhaps leading the way in providing auditoriums for our public schools. It is a good thing and I would

very much favour seeing an auditorium in every one of our schools, in the community centres at least.
I now come to step No. 2. I would say that the next important thing, or possibly just as important as a good general educational program, is a health program. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that in order to have the field and climate in which our artists can prosper and make a living we must have a group of healthy and happy Canadians who can enjoy the work of those artists when it is made available. We look around us and we see the need for research in arthritis, for example, and the need for research in the field of cancer and the fields of heart trouble. I am not belittling what this government is doing at the present time but I think we all agree that they are not doing enough. If we stop and look sanely at this I think most of us would say that until we have reached the stage where we can say to ourselves, we are taking advantage of all the research facilities that we have or that are necessary in this country, we should not be spending the people's money in the promotion of the fine arts.
In my third step I should like to come to something else. In order to give to those artists the security and the opportunities they require, we as individuals must attend concerts. These concerts cost money. You cannot go to hear a great violinist or go to see the Winnipeg ballet, for instance, for 60 cents or 75 cents. Therefore, my third requisite is that we must have economic and financial policies in this country which will assure to our people a way of life which will provide them with sufficient money to patronize the work of those artists, to attend the concerts of those great artists and to give them the encouragement and financial support which is necessary to enable them to stay in this country.
I would stress these things, Mr. Chairman: Assistance and a program of education from the schoolhouse to the university and beyond; a health program that will satisfy all the needs of research in this country; and, lastly, economic policies which will guarantee to each one of us a way of life and an income which will enable us to spend a part of that income to assist financially those artists in earning their own living.
I maintain, as our leader said the other day, that in considering the over-all picture in this country priorities must play a very important part. The things I have mentioned, Mr. Chairman, are priorities which I maintain should be given first consideration. If we reach a stage where we are satisfied that
Canada Council
we have provided our people with these three basic needs, then, and then only, should we proceed to spend $50 million to promote artists who at the present time, by admission of the various speakers, have been forced to leave our shores for the financial support they find in other parts of the world.
I just want to say a word or two on clause (b) of the resolution. Under this clause, Mr. Chairman, $50 million will be made available for assistance to the universities. Looking at it from that point of view, a rather noble one, nothing is more needed by the universities of this country. There is not a university in Canada which is able to provide the facilities it would like to provide and which the people are demanding, not for fine arts but to further the basic education which is required by Canadians to lead them to a better way of life and higher standards of health, to prepare them to go into industrial, research and developmental fields and those areas of endeavour which will provide those things to which the people of Canada are entitled and which our great resources and the ability of our people to exploit them entitle us to enjoy. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am not against voting $50 million for our universities, but when the $50 million is to be narrowed to capital expenditures for the promotion of the fine arts then I say, in the words of our leader, that we must consider the matter of priorities.
I would say that dental colleges, engineering schools and various other schools and faculties which each hon. member of this house could mention are more entitled to consideration from this government at the present time. And yet, when we ask for these things, we are frequently told, "Oh no, we do not have the money for that; we would infringe on the rights of the provinces."
While I welcome the grant of $50 million to universities I must say I cannot see the need of putting it in the hands of a council. Why cannot it go to the national conference of Canadian universities; are they not able to spend this amount of money? Must we set up another board? I think it is ridiculous, Mr. Chairman, and if it were not such a serious matter in the minds of the people of Canada I think we should laugh the establishment of a council out of existence.
I am not going to belabour you further with my comments, Mr. Chairman, but I have simply attempted to express the idea that in order for culture to flourish, grow and achieve proper fruition we must provide the proper climate in which it can develop.

The national research council has not been doing exactly what is to be provided for under this bill, but it is pursuing a similar objective in the scientific field by ways that were, at the time the council was set up, felt to be appropriate. I think it will be necessary to continue and expand the encouragement given in the scientific field, including the four branches the hon. gentleman has mentioned, in order to provide adequately for the material progress which is taking place in this country.
The hon. gentleman will have noticed that the appropriations for the national research council have been steadily increasing and that they have contributed to capital investment of some universities because there were special things required to carry out the kind of research work which the national council wished them to do for the general benefit of

the Canadian economy. That will have to be continued, but that is a field where appeals to private enterprise and private industry have been much more effective than appeals for the development of the facilities for the humanities and social sciences in our universities.
I know of cases, and I am sure the hon. member does also, where pledges for the establishment of what was required in the form of buildings and equipment for engineering have been obtained readily from those who recognize that the companies for which they are responsible will not be able to prosper and develop if there is not that kind of executive ability available for them in succeeding generations. The same with respect to sociology-it is not for the purpose of giving advice to one little group; it is the general theory of the best way to organize co-operative effort between human beings to produce the best results and have them widely distributed.
There is another aspect, psychology, which is assuming a recognized importance in many fields of human endeavour, particularly in the treatment of some forms of mental disturbance and of habits that are detrimental to the individual and embarrassing to society at large. I think a nation making the material progress that our nation is making at the present time owes it to itself and to the world community to be doing its part in the development of these general sciences that know no national border and that will become available to humanity at large.
Of course everything cannot be done at once. In another zone that is one of the worrisome things at the present time. Perhaps there are too many things in the way of capital investment and capital increment being attempted to be done at once, but here is something which the hon. gentleman who has just spoken will recognize as being of real value. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the beginning of the present session several members have dealt with our educational problems from various angles and occasionally in unusual ways. In doing so, they chose to repeat in their own way the cries of alarm being raised by educationists, students and even ordinary mortals in expressions of views which are sometimes modest, sometimes unusual but always significant.
Mr. Chairman, anyone closely or even remotely interested in the things of the mind sadly but undespairingly recognizes the existence of a crisis in higher learning in this country.
All right-thinking people, and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), know that our cultural progress must be on a par with the advances we have made in the economic field.
Thus it is recognized that there is a crisis on the one hand and that, on the other hand, it is urgent to stimulate the two main cultures of Canada, the sources of its influence, its wealth and its continued well-being.
All who deal with the subject strive to outdo one another. Public opinion is aroused, pressures are exerted, influences and interventions are being felt from all sides, ink flows, tongues loosen, deeds multiply, a state of emergency is declared, there is a rush towards public powers, and, as a last resort, an appeal to the Sovereign, because private enterprise cannot do any more.
Fortunately the government of this country has long realized the seriousness of the problem. With cautious reserve and wisdom, it made known its cultural policy. While recognizing to the provinces the exclusive right to legislate in the working out of the school curriculums, in the establishment of the administrative system and school attendance, and in the provision of appropriate sanctions for the application of their legislation in the areas under their jurisdiction, the federal government, for its part, has persistently asserted its absolute right to levy indirect taxes for all purposes, and direct taxes designed to supplement the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The consolidated revenue fund is surely not created and maintained for the purpose of hoarding public funds. On the contrary, the

Canada Council
duty of the state is to contribute to general welfare and to provide for the material, intellectual and moral needs of the nation.
So, Mr. Chairman, it was in that spirit and in the fulfilment of its primary duty that, among other substantial and traditional contributions, the federal government established the National Museum and intends to create additional ones at this very session; that it established the National Research Council through which it has helped and continues to help individuals and private institutions anxious to make scientific discoveries; that each year the departments of Agriculture, of Labour, of Fisheries and of Transports distribute grants, subsidies and scholarships for cultural purposes; that the department of National Health and Social Welfare helps to produce and improve laboratory equipment, to pay tuition fees in connection with training courses in public health or for research purposes in that same field; that grants to voluntary groups as well as scholarships for studies in Europe have been paid and that the subsidies granted to the conference of universities have been increased from $8 to $16 million.
It is still for the sake of culture and for the common good that our government submits today to the consideration of the house its resolution for the establishment in Canada of a Council of arts, humanities and social sciences provided with an endowment fund and with the money necessary for the expansion of our universities until 1967.
All this, Mr. Chairman, is a practical answer to the expressions of alarm to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks on the crisis in higher education in Canada. All this, Mr. Chairman, proves that our country, which has become an international power, does not wish to be solely an economic power but entertains the legitimate ambition, one formally recommended by the papacy, to become a spiritual power among the free nations. It is proud to do this for the good of the world and for the sake of universal peace.
In its declaration published on the 20th of November 1956 on good citizenship and Christianity, the Canadian hierarchy, dealing with the civil power and common good, stated:
Leaders responsible for political society must therefore not attempt to ensure the particular good of everyone, but to establish external and social conditions which will allow everyone to attain, through his own efforts, that degree of human perfection to which he may legitimately aspire.
Mr. Chairman, in the name of an enlightened patriotism, it is time, indeed it is urgent that a change of attitude take place in some quarters which give signs of what

I would call a baneful emotionalism, detrimental to the physical, moral and intellectual development of our student population. If it is true that the federal government has no right to control (and I do say control) education, we must recognize that, under the Canadian constitution of 1867, the federal government has the duty, and even the obligation, to take an interest in education and adequately to promote a higher level of education, of teaching, of instruction and of culture in the various provinces which make up our Canadian nation.
No one can question in good faith the power of the federal parliament to allot, as it sees fit, the general public funds. In fact, our constitutional jurists made the necessary distinction between the power to legislate and the power to spend money.
It is in the light of that essential and basic distinction that the classical colleges for young men and young women of the province of Quebec made the following submission in their brief to the Royal commission on constitutional problems:
If the various governments provided by the Canadian constitution-federal and provincial governments-are both autonomous, they are also co-ordinated in the achievement of a single objective, in that they are complementary to each other and that only the co-ordination of their activities can result in the general welfare of the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, how is that co-ordination of activities to be achieved when, for unavowed and unavowable purposes, provincial authorities are too often prone to complain that their autonomy is being encroached upon? After all, what is autonomy if not, as stated in the dictionary, "the freedom left to the provinces by the central power to administer their internal affairs according to their own laws"?
Now then, is there in Quebec provincial legislation prohibiting the central power from spending part of its public moneys to the benefit of universities and other institutions of cultural or scientific learning? No, Mr. Chairman, there is no such legislation. Besides, according to the constitution, it could not remain on the statute books.
On the contrary, the school code of the province of Quebec, which contains the public education act, provides in section 236 that:
236. It shall be the duty of the school boards In each municipality:
2. to acquire and hold for the corporation all movable and immovable property, moneys or income, and to apply the same for the purposes for which they are intended.
And further on, section 461 of this act provides:
461. In every municipality, all sums of money which have not been specially appropriated by provision of the donors, vendors, or others, shall form S common fund for all the schools . . .

It will be seen, Mr. Chairman, that provincial autonomy allows administrators to accept not only those moneys provided by all sources but makes it a duty for them to acquire, to possess and to use them to the ends provided.

subtopic: LIFE UNDERWRITERS ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: LIFE UNDERWRITERS ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to amend the act incorporating the Life Underwriters Association of Canada which was passed in 1924. The bill relates to only one matter, namely the removal of the dollar maximum value on the property that the association is entitled to hold. In the act of incorporation a maximum value of $100,000 was set.
The bill arises out of the purchase by the association in 1955 of a piece of property in Toronto at 224-226 Richmond street west.
Private Bills
The property was purchased for $85,000. Since that time there has been a considerable rise in real estate values in many areas in Toronto, particularly in this area; and there are indications that if certain large companies obtain permission to construct on University avenue, which is only one block away, there will be a still further rise.
The bill is not prejudicial or objectionable to the province of Ontario because this association, as is required of all dominion corporations, has obtained a licence in mortmain to hold the land in question. The licence obtained in this case is a specific licence so that no matter what the value of the property may be at the present time, the holding of the property is not invalidated by its exceeding the value on which the fee was based. It only means that if the value of the property goes up, the association will be obliged to pay an additional fee.
Hon. members may note that the bill is retroactive in effect. The reason for this is that it is considered desirable to cover any possibility that the value of the property at the present time exceeds the $100,000 maximum set. No one knows precisely what the value of the property is because there has been no valuation made at the present time but it was thought that it could do no harm to put in the provision which in effect made the amendment retroactive.
Hon. members will also note that in the proposed bill there is no maximum value set on the property that the association may hold. That matter was considered and I think principally for three reasons it was decided to submit to this house the provision which does not fix the maximum value. One reason was that it would provide a little bit of difficulty to know what proper maximum should be set. The association does not wish to be obliged to come back to this house and to make another application, with the expense and time involved. In addition, it was considered that there were sufficient safeguards in the act of incorporation itself to make it unnecessary to fix a maximum. The corporation is limited to holding land required for the actual use and occupation of the association or necessary or requisite for the carrying out of its objectives. It was thought that would effectively prevent the corporation from acquiring land for speculative purposes.
I should perhaps have mentioned the fact that the property in question was acquired for the use of the association itself as an office building. In recent years there have been a number of acts passed by this house in which there was no maximum limitation set on the value of the land to be held. I mention the Canadian Nurses' Association act

Private Bills
of 1947, the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association act of 1948. The latest act which I have been able to find was the North American Baptists incorporation act of 1954. I believe there are other examples that might be cited. If hon. members feel that the bill is not objectionable in principle, it will be referred to the appropriate committee. At that time hon. members will have the opportunity of obtaining any additional information they may desire from Mrs. Helen Tedman who is the solicitor for the association and Mr. Leslie W. Dunstall, the executive vice president and from any others the committee may desire to hear.

There will be no pecuniary remuneration for the services rendered other than to the chairman, the vice chairman, the director and the assistant director. The others will receive merely their travelling expenses in attending the meetings. It will be a service that I think the Canadians who will be invited by the government to form part of the council will feel is of real value to their fellow citizens, and of such a character that it will be a tribute to them to be invited to perform it. I want to renew the assurance that the selection of those who will serve will be made without any consideration being given to party political affiliations. I want to assure the house that I will do my best to see that we get the kind of council that will have real prestige with the Canadian public, and will provide a very convenient channel for those who feel they will want to make some substantial contribution to the furtherance of the objectives for which the council is

created. I would hope to see this endowment grow, and perhaps in the first years I would hope some would feel that, instead of adding to the permanent endowment, they should add to the income of the endowment for expenditure in the current year or years.

There are a great many public spirited citizens of Canada who, I think, share the views to which I am giving imperfect expression, and who feel that there is the need for attention being given to that phase of Canadian development. We know that at the present time the prestige of Canada throughout the world stands at a high level because no one has any misgivings about our ambitions or about the possibility of our wishing to exercise undue influence over others.
I think the development that will be brought about by stimulating this phase of Canadian activities will not fail to add to the prestige of Canada. I am not speaking of the prestige of Canada because of any pride or anything of that kind, but I think the prestige of Canada is something that is useful in the political atmosphere of the whole world, because it so happens that in no part of the world are there misgivings about the ambitions of Canada as a nation.

The feature of the plan which worries me is the fact that parliament is to have no control over these activities for a period of some years. The Prime Minister has just said that when the grants to universities are under consideration he hopes there will be a discussion of the work of the Canada Council, but I point out to him that the ordinary yearly grants to universities have nothing to do with the Canada Council. They are made direct to the national conference of universities, and I feel we would find we would be out of order in discussing the activities of the Canada Council under that vote.
Once more I suggest to the Prime Minister that the problem could be met by having a vote, even though it is a small vote, brought in each year in the estimates. This would make it possible to have a discussion of this matter. The Prime Minister seems to be afraid that the appointees to this council will not wish to accept appointments if parliament is to review every year what they do. I believe their reaction will be just the opposite. They will like to have their work made known in parliament and made known across the country as the result of discussion here.

After all, there is no reason why they should be above having their work discussed in parliament. The Prime Minister will, I feel, admit that in the case of all boards or bodies of this kind, their work is reviewed in parliament each year in a very sympathetic and understanding way. I feel confident that men of the calibre who will serve on this council will be only too glad to have their work reviewed here every year and to get suggestions from the members of the house. I hope the government will give consideration to some plan of that kind, which will make it possible to have a discussion every year on the floor of this house concerning the activities of this council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I have listened to the explanation of the Prime Minister concerning the reason the present system of endowment is being set up rather than provision for an annual budget being presented to parliament. Frankly, I am not impressed with the reasons given by the Prime Minister. They seem to lack cogency and force, and they are certainly not based on the experience Britain has had in connection with a similar body.
As the Prime Minister mentioned the other day, Britain set up an arts council. It was established in 1946 by royal charter, and consists of not more than 16 honorary members appointed by the chancellor of the exchequer in consultation with the minister of education and the secretary of state for Scotland. Its main duties are to increase the accessibility of fine arts to the public; to improve the standards in the fine arts, and to advise and co-operate with government departments and other organizations in any way connected directly or indirectly with these projects. There is an amount annually voted to the British council by parliament. It amounts, at the present time, to some $2.5 million a year, and is determined afresh every year. The council presents to the chancellor itemized accounts of the subsidies believed necessary to maintain the organizations and carry into effect the responsibilities of the council.
When the Massey commission made its report, above everything else it demanded, in effect, that parliament should not be circumvented by setting up an organization which would have no direct responsibility to parliament. At page 377, without quoting again this part in its entirety, the report says:
We should also consider it a misfortune if this Canada council became in any sense a department of government, but we realize that since this body will be spending public money it must be in an effective manner responsible to the government and hence to parliament.
Canada Council
Then a little later on, at page 382, it says this:
... we do not doubt that there would be public support of parliamentary action in making adequate funds available to it. We do not find it possible to propose specific sums; we should, however, imagine that the council would find it possible to perform its varied duties effectively with an annual budget . . .
I cannot appreciate the explanation given by the Prime Minister. It looks very much as if the government finds itself more or less embarrassed by the size of the surplus it has this year, and is taking this means of disposing of it to the extent of $50 million.
In so far as this council is concerned, I can see no reason why parliament should be denied, as it will be denied, control year by year over the expenditure, and any say whatsoever over the conduct of the council in the discharge of its responsibilities. Certainly our experience in recent years in the setting up of crown corporations and the like has been that more and more of those crown corporations become independent of parliament and make but a perfunctory report either through the instrumentality of the examination by the Auditor General or in the form of an annual report.
The result is that parliament more and more ceases to have the power and authority to examine the expenditures of money advanced by the people of Canada. Certainly the trend that has been so apparent in recent years toward circumventing parliamentary control by the setting up of governmental bodies ostensibly responsible to the government and to parliament, but in effect not responsible to parliament, must have been in the minds of the Massey commission. After extensive consideration that commission recommended that this council should be required by annual grants to owe a responsibility to parliament.
I can see nothing in the arguments advanced by the Prime Minister that in any way detracts from, or lessens the need, of parliament having an overriding control by examination and consideration of the estimates year by year. I certainly am in favour of the setting up of this council. It is needed. The work it will do is necessary for Canada and its prestige; but there is no need, however beneficial the organization may be and will be, to set aside parliamentary control. This is but another example of the accelerating rate at which parliament more and more becomes less and less important as organizations are set up that become little governments unto themselves.
I ask the Prime Minister to give reconsideration to this. The Massey commission

Canada Council
considered it at length. Five years have gone by without action. Now when action is taken one of the major recommendations of that commission is being ignored. Why should the government in its wisdom that parliamentary control, indirect as well as direct, will be restored by the simple expedient of requiring the council each year to place before the house and the country a statement of its stewardship and its requirements for the ensuing year. Certainly the fortuitous circumstance of the death of very wealthy men is no answer. Parliament of its own volition should not cancel out its duty of making careful examination of moneys voted by parliament to assure that they are satisfactorily expended and are subject to the examination of the people's representatives.

Good things are not always recognized as good things by everybody at the same time. It takes some time for public opinion to bring itself to realize that and to support them. I would imagine that there would now be almost universal support for the council. We have heard some criticism in this house; but there will be the same percentage of support for this council among the Canadian public, whether that part of the public calls itself Liberal, Progressive Conservative or C.C.F. It may not be so with the other group, if we are to judge by the opinions we have heard expressed here; but this is something to be regarded not as a political question in the ordinary sense. It is going to be regarded as something that parliament generally, in its appreciation of the circumstances of the day, looks upon as a wise step to take at this period of our development.

Why should there be this endowment instead of the requirement of having an annual vote recommended? Personally I did not feel that the members of this council should be in the position where the government of the day-whether it be this government or a government formed by my hon. friend, if that ever happens, or formed by some other group in the house- would be able to say, "Well, now, this is the situation. the people of Canada as a whole are too well informed about what it all means. I think perhaps the people as a whole understand the phraseology used respecting the arts.

When it comes to the terminology "social sciences," I am not sure that the general public readily understands what is meant by that term. If one has had anything to do with education, with public school life, high school life or university life, one would perhaps readily recognize what is meant by the social sciences.
I have one or two comments to make with respect to the social sciences that are taught under what is known as the system of progressive education. I hold in my hand a book which was given to me entitled "Education or Indoctrination" by Mary L. Allen. The story was written as the result of considerable discussion that took place in the city of Pasadena, California, concerning their local educational activities; and the book itself, of course, lays the foundation for the story. It appears that the people of the city of Pasadena became so incensed at the inroads socialist thought was making into their educational system that they made an issue of it, the result of which was that many educationists had to resign their posts. I may say something about that a little later.
In reading this book through I came to a very pertinent paragraph in respect to what are termed the social sciences, generally speaking. The paragraph appears at page 24 and reads:
In 1940 Dr. Ralph Robey made an examination of 600 social science textbooks in high schools. He declared, "A substantial portion of the social science textbooks now used in high schools tend to criticize our form of government and hold in derision or contempt the system of private enterprise. . . . There is a notable tendency in the books to play down what has been accomplished in this country and to stress the defects of our democracy.
In that paragraph lies a great story. I agree with that definition, for I personally have read some of the social science textbooks which my children have brought home from high school and public school, though in the public schools the subject is much more simplified. It is a subtle sort of thing; it is something that is difficult to combat. Nevertheless in principle that paragraph gives the explanation of what I would call the damage that can be done by a type of socialist thinking that is beginning to permeate our educational institutions.
So much for the arts and so much for the social sciences. How about the humanities?

What I refer to is the study and, I hope as a result of the study, the acquired knowledge of the treasures that have been provided by the experience, studies and philosophies of past generations. I mean that general knowledge of proper human behaviour that results from the accumulated experience of mankind since history has commenced to be written and not those special things that prepare for the exercise of a special avocation or profession. I mean the general broadening and training of the human mind so that the human individual whose mind it is may have as great benefit as one can derive from the accumulation of lore and knowledge over the centuries.
