I wonder if that is a sound view, and if there is not going to be a great deal of work to be done in the early stages in setting up this council and launching it on its tasks, so much so that the burdens in the early days may be even heavier than they will be later when the council is well launched on its way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
It may well be that for the first few weeks there will be quite a lot of time required, while the council, with the assistance of the investment committee, will be determining what investments should be made of the endowment. I expect that those who will have the responsibility of making the investments, when there will not be the usual restrictions that are placed upon trust companies, will want to give the matter very careful consideration and will endeavour to spread the investments over a pretty wide field so that anything happening in one field will not have the result of a jolt against someone who is carrying all his eggs in one basket. This will probably be quite a serious job that might take quite a lot of time until the investments have been made.
As to the amount to be treated as university grants, that will be only in security funds or securities guaranteed by the government of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I and my colleagues in this group are pleased that at long last the government has decided to take some action to establish the Canada Council. I am a little bit surprised that the chairman has allowed the debate to range as widely as it has. We have had debates under this resolution on federal aid for all sorts of things in the field of education, many of which have had very little to do with the resolution which is now before the committee. This resolution certainly has very little indeed to do with the subject of federal aid for education, or even federal grants to universities in the field of education.
I was, therefore, very pleased to hear the answer the Prime Minister gave to the hon. member for Fort William. When the hon. member for Fort William rose in his place he seemed to indicate that the resolution had something to do with reducing the fees that ordinary university students would be paying. The resolution has nothing whatsoever to do with that, and I was very pleased to hear the Prime Minister so inform the hon. member for Fort William.
However, we welcome the resolution. For many years now the people of this new

nation of ours, the people of Canada, have learned how to earn a living, and I think we have done remarkably well at that. At least, in relation to other peoples of the world, we certainly know how to earn a living. Now we have decided at long last to spend a little bit of money on learning how to live. We have the book which I am sure we all read which says that man does not live by bread alone.
All of us have met many immigrants in recent years, and those immigrants are the first to admit that the people in Canada certainly know how to earn a living. However, in relation to the peoples of western Europe, at least the peoples of the Mediterranean area, the Canadian people have yet to learn the art of living. We have one major conflict of two ideologies in the world today, the ideology of the communist world and the ideology of the capitalist world, both of which have their basis in materialism. To the philosopher there is very little difference basically between the two. The worship of the dollar is not much above the worship of a political machine.
The amount that is being recommended in the resolution is not as much as it seems. I know $100 million sounds like a lot of money in many parts of Canada and to many of the people of Canada. We must remember that half of it is to go for the erection of university buildings; the other half is to be put into a fund. When you look at the income the Canada Council will have from this $50 million a year you will see that it amounts to only slightly over 10 cents per capita per year. I do not think the average Canadian will resent overly much being taxed to the extent of having 10 cents of his income spent by the federal government on the encouragement of the arts, the humanities and the social sciences.
I regret that in the speeches I have heard so far from the government benches all indications are that the breadth of the effort upon which we are about to embark is to be rather limited. The Prime Minister himself, I think for some reasons maybe known only to himself, emphasized a week or so ago that in years gone by those who had patronized the arts were also those who, to use his words, "knew the value of gold coins".
I read a lot into that sentence of the Prime Minister. If the Prime Minister meant by it that the men in days gone by who had gold coins were the ones who had the leisure to interest themselves in the arts, I can agree with him. However, if the Prime Minister meant that there was any correlation at all between the ability to acquire money and the ability to appreciate the worth-while
Canada Council
things in life, I must take exception; because even among the limited number of people whom I know are people who know something of the art of living, but they are not at all necessarily those who know something of the art of how to climb onto the backs of their fellow men and get a free ride.
The Prime Minister also referred to his desire not to establish a Canada arts council which would be superimposing itself upon some of the efforts which are being made in the field of the development of the arts in Canada. Once again I must give him the benefit of the doubt. If the Prime Minister meant by the word "superimposing" that he did not like the idea of superimposing something upon organizations which were already well established, and that he did not feel the new Canada Council should attempt to shove any form of culture down the throats of Canadian people, of course I must agree with him. However, if he meant that the whole of the energies of the Canada Council to be established were to be devoted only to assisting those major national organizations which now exist, then once again I have to take exception to that.
In its report at page 373 the Massey commission had this to say:
We are faced, it seems to us, by a threefold problem: cultural activity within Canada, cultural relations abroad, Canada's relationship with UNESCO.
Well, Mr. Chairman, in the minutes left to me I mean to devote my thoughts to cultural activity within Canada. As far as cultural relations abroad and Canada's relationship with UNESCO are concerned, I must admit that I know very little indeed about this matter; and unlike some of the "socreds" in this house I am unwilling to look for communist-makers under every bedspread that we may have in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: You are just blind like that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
With respect to cultural activity in Canada the royal commission went on to say:
When national policy for development of the arts, letters and sciences in Canada is devised, first consideration should be given to the specific and peculiar needs of Canada, and only secondary consideration should be given to the application of policies and methods adopted by other countries for the solution of their specific and peculiar cultural problems.
I would like to say "amen" to that recommendation. I heartily agree that in the development of Canadian culture very serious attention should be paid to the peculiar problems we have in Canada, and we should not simply ape the efforts of western European nations.

Canada Council
I referred a moment ago to those of my colleagues in the house who belong to the Social Credit party. I can well remember as a young man listening to the ranting and raving of the late Premier William Aberhart-

speechtext: -about the 50 big shots of Canada. I was extremely amazed the other day in listening to the remarks of the Social Credit leader in this debate. I thought the Prime Minister made a very sensible contribution when he offered for our consideration the thought that in centuries gone by there had been many men of wealth who had agreed to be patrons of the arts.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. You will recall, sir, that not long ago the chairman referred to the wide field over which this debate was ranging. He said that in his judgment we should not refer even to UNESCO. I wonder what this particular line of thinking has to do with the resolution we are considering. I have no objection, sir, to allowing this discussion to go as far afield as you like; but I would suggest that if you are going to allow the hon. member to address his remarks in a purely provincial political atmosphere, then you should not try to prevent others from extending the scope of the debate, too,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was just about to refer to the contribution to this debate made by the leader of the Social Credit party on January 18 last, when he expressed regret that there were not more extremely wealthy people in this country. I shall quote the remarks of the hon. member as reported at page 407 of Hansard for that date:
I am going to say to you, Mr. Chairman, that if we had in our country more people of material substance I am quite satisfied that they would be just as generous as the people in the United States have been, but one of the great reasons why we do not have as many wealthy people here, and I think we should begin looking into this, is that we have followed taxation policies that have taken the material substance away from people who would be patrons of the arts and sciences and have left them with little or nothing with which to endow. It is high time we began to take a careful look at what the real effects of our taxation policies have been.
Well, Mr. Chairman, here we have inside of 22 years a complete turnabout. In 1935 their leader ranted and raved about the 50 [DOT]big shots and-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: No ranting, no raving.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: -today their leader complains that we have not enough multimillionaires in Canada to patronize the arts.

speechtext: Of course that is entirely wrong.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River, who is interrupting, comes from Alberta and I think I can readily understand his thinking. I come from British Columbia, where we are used to the fact that multimillionaires have found their way into the Social Credit party.

speechtext: What about Alberta?

speechtext: They have all kinds of oil rights.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Culture is something that
cannot be bought. I was very pleased indeed to see that the Prime Minister used the word "encouragement" in the resolution. The purpose of the council is for the encouragement of the arts, humanities and social sciences. The main theme of my contribution is a plea that this effort be spread for the benefit of the masses of the people of Canada. I regret very much that most of the addresses I have heard in this debate so far from almost all sections of the house have created in me the impression that most hon. members seem to think this $100 million is going to be spent on the experts in the arts in Canada. I think the need existing among the masses of the people is much more urgent than the need existing among the experts.
In most parts of industrialized Canada we have the 40-hour week. When we read the report of the Gordon commission and the representations made by the labour unions of Canada we realize the day is not far distant when we will be talking about a 30-hour week, and that causes me some serious concern.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Not me; I would love it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I know the hon. member for Kootenay East, being a so-called union leader, pretends not to be afraid of this; however, I know that upon serious and sober reflection even he will consider as serious a matter which I think ought to be raised in this debate. If we are going to reduce the 40-hour work week to a 30-hour work week we have to be sure that the Canadian people can absorb all the effects created by a 30-hour work week.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Keep socialism out of it and it will be all right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
We are today a nation of sitters and a nation of viewers. As far as the

development of the individual is concerned, television can be a curse as well as a blessing. The people of Canada will sit and listen to the radio and will watch sports rather than participating in sports. The people of Canada will watch drama on television rather than participating in human life. I submit once again, Mr. Chairman, there is a responsibility which this parliament must face in this regard. It is for that reason I sincerely welcome this effort by the government to help the Canadian people to learn how to live.
I deeply regret that in my home city of New Westminster, British Columbia, on a single night more people will attend one hockey game than you will find the following Sunday at all the churches in the whole city combined, and at all the political meetings for a 10-year period combined.
I think it is high time we paid some serious attention to these problems. When we spend $100 million of the taxpayers' money for the encouragement of the arts, the humanities and the social sciences let us make sure that at least some of that money is spent for the benefit of the broad masses of the Canadian people. I submit that the people who get themselves elected to this parliament should have some understanding of the problems which I am attempting to outline at this time.
In my riding of Burnaby-Coquitlam there are many cultural activities being carried on. In Burnaby, loco, Port Moody and Coquitlam there are hundreds of small groups of people working together in order to raise the cultural level of our society. At the present time these people are receiving no national direction, guidance or encouragement. I hope when the bill which will follow this resolution passes it will provide for the giving to my people back home of a little of the encouragement, leadership and guidance for which they are looking.
I am thinking also of the broad picture of Canada. Canada is made up of people who speak two main languages, but dozens of other racial groups are making their contributions. If the Canada Council could broaden its concept of its responsibilities it could do much toward promoting the idea of national unity, and at the same time ensure that many of the contributions which these people have to make will not be lost.
I am thinking also of the field of adult education, and am hoping that it will not be relegated to a secondary position. In the area I represent I think I am safe in saying that there are practically as many people taking part in adult education at the present time as there are pupils in the elementary and high schools. Vancouver is fast gaining
Canada Council
a world-wide reputation for its adult education program. Largely responsible for the progressive outlook of the people of the Scandinavian countries is the fact that in many of those countries the people never stop going to school, and are still learning even when they become grandfathers and grandmothers.
I should like to refer to the second section of the resolution, and note that when the Prime Minister spoke on January 18, as reported on page 397 of Hansard of that date, he said that the contribution would be not more than 50 per cent in any case. He was referring to the capital grants to universities. The other day, and again today, the Prime Minister made it perfectly clear that these capital grants have nothing whatsoever to do with the ordinary functions of our Canadian universities.
If the Canada Council should find it expedient to utilize a Canadian university in order to accomplish or further one of its aims or objectives and a building were needed, then the Canada Council would be able to say, "We will pay half the capital expenditure." I find that most regrettable, because there are many areas in Canada which are particularly in need of added sources of supply, if you like to put it that way, of economic well-being.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me? If I gave the impression that the capital fund could be used only for special projects which the council wanted to have carried out I misled the house, because the bill as drafted provides that the council can make grants of half the cost of any building or capital equipment required to promote the study and enjoyment of the arts, the humanities and the social sciences.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the Prime Minister for clarifying his statement somewhat, but I still must point out that even in the statement the Prime Minister made just now he has made it clear that the 50 per cent will have nothing whatsoever to do with what are considered by most people of Canada to be the ordinary functions of a university.
If the Canada Council should desire that certain projects be undertaken at a certain university which involved certain capital expenditures, then the council might contribute 50 per cent of those expenditures. I hope I am being fair to the sentiments of the Prime Minister. I read carefully what he said the other day; but I have noticed, as I said when I began my remarks, that much of the debate has run far afield from the

Canada Council
limitations set by the resolution and by what the Prime Minister said. However, that is beside the point.
The main point I wanted to make with the Prime Minister was that this idea of matching grants works a hardship on many of the provinces. It works a hardship on all the have-not provinces, which include four Atlantic provinces and perhaps the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. I submit that basically this principle of matching grants-and I submit that is what he did propose-perpetuates an evil which already exists in connection with our university grants, and we should not compound that evil by making it applicable in this particular field. If we want to develop the arts, humanities and social sciences I cannot think of a more suitable place than some of the universities in some of the have-not provinces.
I should like to pose this question to the Prime Minister. Why 50 per cent? Why not 100 per cent? If a need is recognized by the to be established Canada Council,. why should not the council assume the whole cost? Why should not the council have the right to determine where in Canada would be the most suitable location? As the Prime Minister has put it, I can very well see the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia obtaining concessions by way of capital grants while the other provinces, because they have not the matching money, would be denied that benefit'.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I wish to ask a question of the Prime Minister. I suppose, in every organization, the man who heads it is of great importance, and I cannot imagine an organization where the top man would be of greater importance than in the case of the Canada Council. Is it possible for the Prime Minister to answer this question? In his thinking about the qualifications desirable for this position, does it seem to him that executive and administrative qualities are required, or is he looking for a man who would give the council intellectual and, shall I say, aesthetic leadership? I realize that one cannot divide men sharply into two classes, and I realize that the Prime Minister may get a man who, happily, combines both qualities; but certainly it is of importance, and it would be of great interest to me, to know whether the Prime Minister in approaching the search for this man has in mind rather the one type or the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: What I had in mind, Mr. Chairman, was this; a man who would have drive, energy and vision; a man who would make the project active and see to it that the whole council got the benefit of the wisdom that each of its members could contribute to its deliberations. And I would be pleased, too, if it were someone who could take his part of the responsibility in making investments with endowment dollars in a wise way during this period of rapid development of Canadian enterprise, and who could also visualize the effect upon the Canadian nation of a stimulus to these-I use the word which the hon. gentleman does not like any better than I do-so-called cultural activities; and he would be a means of bringing out the intellectual contribution that each and every member of the council could make to the conduct of its general affairs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has
used the words "drive, energy and wisdom" which, I am sure, we would all expect to find in regard to any good man. He has given me the impression that what he is really looking for is what may be called an executive type.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

I was not
thinking of someone who would be a specialist in any one of the fields of art, but of one who would have an appreciation of all the contributions that could be made in that field.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question. In my limited experience in the granting of public funds for charitable, artistic and other purposes, it has always seemed to me that the best use was made of those funds if it was a requirement that the persons or organizations to whom they were granted were required to put up a corresponding amount; in other words, that government funds were granted to match funds put up by private individuals and associations who were interested in the same purpose. This seems to give an assurance that the best use will be made not only of private funds but of the additional moneys put up by the government. I wonder if that principle is given any place in the disposition of funds by the Canada Council, apart from the capital grants to universities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: It is, Mr. Chairman, in the case of the capital grants. But it was felt it would be a good, proper stimulus to provide an initial endowment fund amounting to as much as $50 million and created at the expense of the whole Canadian public.

speechtext:
I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, whether the Prime Minister understood my point. If, say, a ballet company which is struggling to establish itself were to ask the Canada Council for a grant, it occurs to me tnat a sound basis of operations would be for the Canada Council to say, "Yes, if you believe sufficiently in this work of yours to provide part of the funds, we will then meet your needs as to the other part of the funds." I suggest this is a much better policy than being too free with public money where there are no private funds ready to support the purpose in hand, and I wonder
Canada Council
if that principle has been given effect to in any way in the present proposals.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: There is no limitation on the council as to how the money should be applied?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

No, none; but the fact that they will be operating in public and that their operations will be reported upon annually by the Auditor General in a report that will be tabled in parliament will ensure that the council is very conscious that the Canadian public will feel that it is their money that is being administered by this council; and they will want, I think, to use it in a manner that will commend itself to the majority of the Canadian people.
